newsitem.title: HONG KONG: HK's Tung votes for stability with choice of team.
newsitem.headline: HK's Tung votes for stability with choice of team.

text.p: A decision by Hong Kong's future leader Tung Chee-hwa to retain most of the territory's top civil servants after the handover to Chinese rule was seen by analysts on Friday as a signal he values stability.
"I think Tung Chee-hwa is keeping an eye on stability more than anything else," said an analyst with a local bank.
"There has been some concern regarding the future of the government in the transition period. And retaining the top officials in the government will help quite a lot in terms of stability," he said.

Hong Kong becomes a Special Administrative Region (SAR) of China at midnight on June 30 after more than 150 years of British rule and Tung will take over from colonial Governor Chris Patten as its first chief executive.
Tung unveiled his post-handover administration on Thursday, with 21 of the 23 posts going to incumbent officials.
Among the civil servants who will keep their jobs is Chief Secretary Anson Chan, Patten's number two, who will become Administrative Secretary under the new regime.
"My principal consideration, firstly, was that they are good, and secondly, that it is most important during the transition that we (have) as minimum changes as possible," Tung said on Thursday.
Roderick Houng-Lee, partner at Price Waterhouse, said the retention of top civil servants was favourable to international investors' confidence in the local economy.
"It has to be good. It would have been a disaster if (Tung) had changed everyone," he said.
Academic Michael DeGolyer, director of a long-term project studying the handover, said it was a wise move to ensure stability and prosperity.
"One thing we can certainly count on is that with no changes in personnel, with no changes in responsibility, the idea of continuity...is certainly borne out," he said.
Rumours that outspoken Financial Secretary Donald Tsang would not make the cut were dispelled with the appointments.
"There were a lot of rumours regarding Donald Tsang and some other officials, but I think that for Tung the decisions were mainly a question of stability," said the bank analyst.
Tsang said on Friday he was a very good friend of Tung and viewed him with considerable respect.
"I of course feel very honoured that I will be able to continue to serve the SAR government. That has been my ambition throughout my working career," Tsang said.

Responding to reports the head of the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA), Hong Kong's de facto central bank, might be appointed by the chief executive in future rather than the financial secretary, Tsang said he was sure Tung would "take the wisest, wisest counsel" in deciding the issue.
Tung said on Thursday he would review the matter of the HKMA appointment with Tsang and Chan.

Some analysts have said that putting the HKMA more directly in the control of the chief executive might dilute the power of the financial secretary, while others saw such a move merely as a way to elevate the HKMA's international status.
Analysts predicted that Tung would keep his top-level team intact for at least a year or two before attempting a major reshuffle.
